text: Every quantum error-correcting code ever built has to work around one unbendable rule. This lesson states that rule precisely and shows exactly how codes get around it without breaking it.

The no-cloning theorem says there is no physical process — no unitary operation, no measurement, no combination of the two — that takes an arbitrary unknown quantum state and produces two independent copies of it while leaving the original intact. This isn't a hardware limitation that better qubits will someday fix; it follows directly from the linearity of quantum evolution. A hypothetical cloning machine that works for ket-zero and ket-one individually can be shown to fail on a superposition of the two — it outputs something else entirely. Crucially, this only forbids copying an unknown state; if you already know you want ten copies of ket-zero, preparing that many is trivial and not cloning at all.

Classical repetition coding depends on the opposite assumption: encoding a bit as three copies only works because a classical bit can be read and copied without disturbing it. No-cloning removes that assumption entirely for quantum information — you cannot take an unknown qubit state and produce three copies of it to vote over later. This is precisely why the classical trick fails at its most basic step.

The resolution is that quantum codes don't copy the logical state — they spread it. Encoding one logical qubit into three physical qubits through an entangling circuit, built explicitly with CNOTs starting next chapter, produces an entangled state where no single physical qubit, and no literal copy of the logical state, exists anywhere. The information lives in correlations between the physical qubits instead. That distinction is exactly what you're allowed to measure: the correlations, through stabilizer and syndrome measurements built starting in Chapter 3, without ever measuring, and therefore without destroying, what alpha and beta actually are.

Next lesson is this chapter's lab: minimum distance, and why a distance-3 code corrects exactly 1 error — a rule every quantum code in this course, including the Steane code in Chapter 4, inherits unchanged.
